Looking Ahead –
Certification, Emerging
Trends, and Next Steps
We are at a place in our journey where we have to stop and ask ourselves, What’s next? Before we do
that, let’s think about where we’ve been.
We’ve learned what Terraform is and how to use it. We’ve learned some basic concepts of cloud
architecture that transcend the particular cloud platform you might be using at the moment. We’ve
built three sophisticated architectures on each of the three major hyperscalers—AWS, Azure, and
GCP—and finally, we’ve learned how to work with existing environments, either importing them into
Terraform or managing them with Terraform as long-lived environments in production or otherwise.
That’s a lot! It’s been quite a journey, so where do we go from here? Well, the answer is in you. I hope
that means you have learned something along this journey, and you’ll take that into your day-to-day
work to build amazing systems that solve real-world problems and are better equipped to build and
manage them with the power of Terraform.
In this chapter, before we close, I’d like to discuss some potential next steps, both for your personal

51898.title: masteringterraform
51898.heading: Chapter 8, where we first went through this transformation on the AWS platform. In the next section,
51898.content:
growth and extended learning. You have invested a tremendous amount of time in reading this book
and have begun your journey of mastering Terraform. You may want to consider certification as a
way to validate your skills and knowledge and to demonstrate your expertise to potential employers.
Additionally, there may be other technologies that you may want to consider as you continue to deepen
your mastery of Terraform. We’ll explore some of these options, including tools and platforms that
complement Terraform and how they can enhance your Infrastructure as Code (IaC) capabilities.
By the end of this chapter, you should have a clear roadmap for your continued learning and a solid
foundation for your future endeavors in the world of cloud infrastructure management.
Looking Ahead – Certification, Emerging Trends, and Next Steps 440
The chapter covers the following topics:
• Preparing for the exam
• Terraform Cloud
• What’s next?
Preparing for the exam
On your journey through this book to mastering Terraform, you’ve gained a wealth of knowledge
and practical experience. But how do you showcase your expertise to the world? One of the most
effective ways is through certification. In this section, we’ll delve into the intricacies of preparing for
the Terraform certification exams. We’ll cover the key topics you need to master, the format of the
exam, and strategies to optimize your study time and approach. By the end of this section, you’ll be well
equipped with the tools and confidence needed to tackle the certification exam and take a significant
step forward in mastering Terraform.
Scope and topics
The HashiCorp Terraform Associate Certification is an entry-level certification that will test you
on general concepts of IaC, Terraform’s competitive position against other tools, working with code
using the HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL), and using the core Terraform workflow as
well as other workflows that are supported through various sub-commands within the Command-
Line Interface (CLI).
There is a new exam that is coming soon called Terraform Authoring and Operations Professional.
This exam is designed for seasoned practitioners who have extensive experience in managing production
systems, developing reusable modules, and operating within a mature enterprise IaC environment. It
aims to validate the advanced skills and deep understanding required to efficiently author and manage
Terraform configurations at scale. Candidates can expect to be tested on their ability to implement
complex infrastructure architectures, optimize workflows, and ensure best practices in an enterprise
environment. This certification is an excellent opportunity for those looking to demonstrate their expertise
in leveraging Terraform’s full capabilities in a sophisticated and dynamic infrastructure landscape.

51899.title: masteringterraform
51899.heading: Chapter 8, where we first went through this transformation on the AWS platform. In the next section,
51899.content:
This book is designed to help you go beyond many of the foundational concepts covered in the
Associate exam and help you prepare for the Professional exam. As a result, our journey in this book
has been taking a hyper-practical approach to building actual cloud architectures using Terraform
and implementing collaborative flows with Terraform and an automation pipeline tool, which, for
the entirety of this book, was GitHub Actions.
Preparing for the exam 441
As you can see in the following diagram, I map chapters within this book to actual topics covered
within the Associate exam:
Figure 18.1 – Map of Associate certification topics to chapters in this book
We breezed through the foundational conceptual layers of IaC, Terraform’s architecture, and HCL in
the first three chapters of this book. This was by design, as this book is intended for an intermediate
to advanced audience and not a beginner’s guide.
This allowed us to dedicate some time, in Chapters 4 through 6, to the conceptual layer that most
Terraform practitioners actually spend their time in—the cloud architectures that they are designing
and provisioning when we set the bases for the cloud computing paradigms we would be working
with across all three clouds.
Then, we hit the ground running, getting our hands dirty and building three real-world solutions for
each cloud. As you can see, we spent most of our time in the book working on implementing HCL code
across all three clouds—AWS, Azure, and GCP—and across three cloud computing paradigms—virtual
machines, containers, and serverless. In these nine solutions, we implemented Terraform modules and
delved deep into configuration using three corresponding Terraform providers: aws, azure, and GCP.
In Chapters 16 and 17, we focused on the non-core workflows involving advanced topics in state
management and configuration importation that are common and necessary when working with
existing environments—whether or not they were originally provisioned with Terraform.
Looking Ahead – Certification, Emerging Trends, and Next Steps 442
In the Professional exam, this is still significant coverage of all the key topics with one key exception:
Figure 18.2 – Map of Professional certification topics to chapters in this book
The notable exception is Terraform Cloud, which I chose to omit as a main focus of this book since
I don’t think knowledge of it is required to master Terraform at this time. We will look at Terraform
Cloud in the next section of this chapter, as I think it is an interesting topic area for further study if
you want to leverage some of its capabilities to streamline your organization’s collaborative workflows.
Preparation
Go and check out the study guides for both the Associate and Professional exams. The study guides
have helpful links to the official documentation, which should augment the contents of this book.

51900.title: masteringterraform
51900.heading: Chapter 8, where we first went through this transformation on the AWS platform. In the next section,
51900.content:
Remember, this book was intended to be a practical guide for those who want to master Terraform
to provision cloud architecture. That doesn’t necessarily mean memorizing every nook and cranny of
the Terraform CLI. I specifically chose to focus on skills that will help you start developing real-world
solutions no matter what cloud and cloud computing paradigm you’ll be working with.
The exam will likely have tricky edge cases or obscure commands that are seldom used, so be ready
for that, but I wouldn’t dedicate a tremendous amount of time to it. Make yourself a quick cheat sheet
of some of these obscure commands and how to use them. Employ flashcards to help you memorize
them if you feel like you need to. If you have a solid understanding of Terraform’s architecture and
are hands-on with it, you should do well.
My best advice is to study through hands-on experience. Take the projects in this book, and feel free
to clone them from my GitHub repositories, but to maximize your own mastery, develop them from
scratch in your own repository on GitHub. Recreate them, provision yourself and the environment, and
then improve upon them. Think about how you would like to modularize components within them to
be more reusable. Go ahead and implement those modules, and then refactor your environment to use
your new modules. Treat your environment as if it were production and try to minimize the impact
on your environment by making sure you avoid replacing resources in your existing environment
while trying to refactor to use your new modules.
Terraform Cloud 443
I sat for the exam while I was at HashiConf in October 2023. I didn’t study, I didn’t prepare, I didn’t
even read the study guide. I passed with a score of 84.21%. I was pretty happy about it. Am I telling
you this to brag? No. Well, maybe a little, but seriously, my point is that the best way for you to
prepare is by doing. How was I able to pass without studying at all? Because I’ve been hands-on with
Terraform for several years and know it inside and out. Did I know every obscure command within
the Terraform CLI? Absolutely not. Had I ever used Terraform Cloud? Not for one New York minute.
You have to ask yourself, do you want to pass an exam, or do you want to upskill yourself and become
a dangerous force in the cloud automation space with one of the most powerful automation tools in
the world? I think the answer is clear. Focus on the primary objective with gazelle-like intensity and
augment it with a bit of studying more obscurities, and you will do well.
Now that you are energized, feeling empowered by all that you have learned from this book, and ready
to take the Terraform Associate or upcoming Professional exam, let’s look forward to some interesting
topics that every Terraformer (not just the Azure ones) should know about.

51901.title: masteringterraform
51901.heading: Chapter 8, where we first went through this transformation on the AWS platform. In the next section,
51901.content:
Terraform Cloud
In this section, we’ll explore Terraform Cloud, a powerful platform designed to enhance Terraform’s
capabilities in team-based and enterprise environments. Terraform Cloud provides a centralized
hub for managing and automating Terraform workflows, offering features such as version control
integration, remote state management, and collaborative IaC development.
We’ll take a brief look at the core components of Terraform Cloud, including advanced features such
as workspace management, private module registry, cost estimation, and policy enforcement.
By understanding Terraform Cloud’s features and use cases, you’ll gain insights into how it can streamline
your infrastructure management processes and foster collaboration among team members. It’s definitely
something to consider if you are looking to scale up your organization’s IaC maturity quickly.
Features
Terraform Cloud’s mission is about streamlining the process of managing environments with IaC. This
will include features that handle day-to-day operation concerns of using Terraform, as well as more
advanced capabilities related to empowering teams and scaling across larger organizations within the
enterprise. The following is a diagram showing the grouping of these capabilities:
Looking Ahead – Certification, Emerging Trends, and Next Steps 444
Figure 18.3 – Terraform Cloud capabilities
These groupings are across four functional areas:
• Core workflow operations
• Organization and logistics
• Module management and publishing
• Day 2 operations support
We’ll explore each of these functional areas individually to get a better idea of what Terraform Cloud
brings to the table.
Core workflow operations
As we know, Terraform, itself is a simple command-line tool that processes HCL code and leverages
a multitude of providers to generate a plan and then execute that plan by orchestrating resource
creation across multiple providers. Terraform Cloud is a multi-tenant SaaS offering that encapsulates
the functionalities of the command-line tool and hosts it as a managed service offering.
As a result, a significant portion of the value of Terraform Cloud comes from, well, Terraform itself—
that is, the command-line tool that does all the work. However, Terraform Cloud provides many things
beyond what is built into the command-line tool. As a hosted service, it sits atop our version control
system and acts as a pipelining tool that executes the Terraform plan and apply commands. In
this book, we worked with GitHub Actions to integrate the Terraform command-line tool into our
workflows to run the core Terraform workflow, which includes plan and apply.
Terraform Cloud’s capabilities in the Core Workflow Operations category focus on providing Terraform
as a service, similar to what pipeline tools such as GitHub Actions do for general-purpose pipelines,

51902.title: masteringterraform
51902.heading: Chapter 8, where we first went through this transformation on the AWS platform. In the next section,
51902.content:
Terraform Cloud 445
but Terraform-specific. This means Terraform Cloud is essentially an automation-hosted platform
that specializes in executing Terraform configurations. As a result, the service is tailored to Terraform’s
specific needs, including things such as remote state management. However, it also includes essential
features found in general-purpose pipelining tools, such as source control integration, cloud platform
credential management, and secure variable storage. It also offers extension points for integration with
external tools, allowing it to be integrated into broader automation orchestration.
Organizational and logistics
The organizational and logistics aspect of Terraform Cloud is designed to facilitate collaboration and
management by teams within organizations large and small. It provides a structured environment to
organize users, roles, and permissions across logical projects, leading to the creation and operation of
Terraform workspaces—ensuring that team members have the appropriate access and permissions to
perform their tasks effectively. Like other more general-purpose automation platforms such as Azure
DevOps and GitHub Enterprise, maintaining order and control in these collaborative environments
is baseline functionality.
Module management and publishing
Terraform Cloud’s capabilities within module management and publishing enable teams and organizations
to build, maintain, and share their own libraries of Terraform modules across their organization. As
we’ve discussed, Terraform modules often encapsulate organizationally approved best practices and
are often maintained by a central organization responsible for their implementation and built-in
quality. Terraform Cloud supports this publishing process by integrating Terraform module testing
and validation to ensure quality before new versions of Terraform modules are distributed across an
organization. Additionally, these modules can be made available in no-code environments, providing
a service catalog-like experience for end users. This empowers teams to standardize and scale their
infrastructure management efforts but also makes the solutions that they build available to parts of
the organization that are unfamiliar with IaC or Terraform in general.
Day 2 operations support
The Day 2 operations support functionality in Terraform Cloud is geared toward managing and
maintaining existing systems in production. It includes continuous validation to ensure environments
remain up to date with the desired state described within the code and drift detection to identify
changes made outside of Terraform code. There are also more advanced enterprise features, such
as audit logging, to help larger organizations meet regulatory compliance standards and implement
risk management policies to detect and prevent unplanned changes to the environment. Another key

51903.title: masteringterraform
51903.heading: Chapter 8, where we first went through this transformation on the AWS platform. In the next section,
51903.content:
feature is the policy-as-code capabilities provided by Sentinel, which enables governance and security
controls over the environments managed by Terraform Cloud.
Looking Ahead – Certification, Emerging Trends, and Next Steps 446
Pricing tiers
The Free tier provides all IaC capabilities of Terraform as a hosted service out of the box and all of
the core workflow operations capabilities—including remote state, secure variable storage, dynamic
provider credentials, and source control integration. It’s a great way to get your feet wet exploring the
platform and learning the new way of working with Terraform Cloud as the foundation as opposed to a
general-purpose pipeline tool. As expected, it is pretty limited with a single concurrent job and limited
access to more advanced enterprise features such as Policy-as-Code and run tasks that are designed
to help you scale Terraform Cloud into a larger, more sophisticated IaC-powered organization. The
Free tier allows you to provision up to 500 resources.
The Standard tier adds team management and increases the number of concurrent jobs from one to
three, which probably makes sense in a team environment. The pricing model is per hour per resource,
which means every resource you declare in your Terraform configuration will count toward your
usage. The price per hour per resource, at the time of writing, was $0.00014. To give you an idea of
how much this would cost to operate, one of the environments that I manage is an environment with
a small Kubernetes cluster and all the surrounding supporting infrastructure. I provisioned exactly
110 resources in this environment using Terraform:
110 resources x $0.00014 per resources per hour = $0.0154 per hour
$0.0154 per hour * 24 hours per day * 30 days per month = $11.088 per month
So, for roughly 11 dollars per month, I can use Terraform Cloud to manage my environment. This is
in addition to what I pay for my source control management system and the cloud hosting costs of
the environment.
The Plus tier introduces Day 2 operations support scenarios such as audit logging, drift detection,
continuous validation, ephemeral workspaces, ServiceNow integrations, and unlimited Policy-as-
Code to help you better manage your environments and integrate with your day-to-day operations.
The Enterprise tier is essentially the hosted offering that allows you to deploy Terraform Enterprise
into your own data center, which can be important to large enterprises that are not interested in taking
advantage of the lowered operating cost of utilizing HashiCorp’s multi-tenant offering, Terraform Cloud.
In this section, we looked at Terraform Cloud, including what it offers in terms of capabilities and
recognizing that, unlike more general-purpose automation platforms, it is tailored specifically for IaC

51904.title: masteringterraform
51904.heading: Chapter 8, where we first went through this transformation on the AWS platform. In the next section,
51904.content:
management and collaboration using Terraform. Compared to these more general-purpose pipeline
tools, Terraform Cloud stands out by offering features specifically designed for Terraform workflows,
such as remote state management, secure variable storage, and integrated module management. This
focus on Terraform-specific functionality makes it an ideal choice for teams looking to take their IaC
processes to the next level. Next, we’ll look at some other key trends to be aware of that are out of the
scope of this book but should be on the radar of anyone looking to truly master Terraform.
What’s next? 447
What’s next?
In this section, we’ll explore some emerging trends within the Terraform community that are essential
for anyone working with Terraform to be aware of. While these topics are technically outside the scope
of this book, including upcoming features that have not even been finalized and may evolve over
time, understanding these emerging topics can provide valuable context into the future direction of
Terraform and help you stay ahead of the curve in your journey to mastering Terraform.
CDK
The Terraform Cloud Development Kit (CDK) is a method for developing Terraform configuration
using imperative programming languages that you already know and use within your application
development. Any language can be used, from Python to C# and from TypeScript to Java. Any Terraform
provider and Terraform modules can be used as well. It’s essentially the same thing as working with
HCL but using the programming language of your choice.
Figure 18.4 – Use the programming language of your choice
Whatever language you choose will ultimately compile down into a Terraform-compatible JSON file
that is then interpreted by Terraform in a similar way as HCL files are processed.
This option is great for existing development teams that already work with a programming language of
choice and don’t want to invest energy in learning the HCL. However, for non-developers, the HCL is
definitely the way to go as it provides a simple, functional language that is easier to adopt and already
has a massive ecosystem of practitioners that are using it, asking and answering questions about it,
and sharing code on public GitHub repositories that can help you along on your way.
Terraform Stacks
Terraform Stacks, a highly anticipated feature on the horizon for Terraform, promises to revolutionize
the way we design and manage complex architectures across multiple control planes. This innovative
feature is expected to provide a seamless and integrated experience for users working with Terraform
Cloud and the Terraform Community Edition (the command-line tool). By allowing for more
sophisticated organization and modularization of IaC, Terraform Stacks aims to streamline the process
of deploying and managing large-scale, multi-tiered environments. We’ll dig into what we know right

51905.heading: Chapter 8, where we first went through this transformation on the AWS platform. In the next section,
51905.content:
Looking Ahead – Certification, Emerging Trends, and Next Steps 448
now based on what was made public by HashiCorp at the time of writing and how it’s supposed to
work when it’s eventually released.
Current state
In the current landscape of Terraform usage, a singular root module serves as the cornerstone of
infrastructure deployment. This root module encompasses the provider configuration and engages
with various Terraform resources, either directly or via module references. The versatility of these
root modules is heightened by supplying them with distinct input parameters tailored to the desired
environment for deployment. To further segregate the deployment of each root module instance,
Terraform workspaces are employed, resulting in individual Terraform state files. These state files
are then uniquely associated with specific environments, such as DEV, TEST, or PROD, effectively
encapsulating the configuration and status of the deployed infrastructure within each environment:
Figure 18.5 – Current state: Terraform workspaces and root modules
In the realm of provisioning complex environments with Terraform, it is often necessary to employ
multiple root modules to delineate layers of architecture based on their dependencies, such as blast
radius considerations or concrete control plane dependencies such as those between a cloud platform
and a Kubernetes control plane. This is not the only scenario where you will run into control plane
dependencies within the providers, but it is a common one as the use of managed Kubernetes offerings
continues to grow in popularity. The dependency can arise anytime you are provisioning resources
with two or more providers and one provider provisions a resource that is then used to configure
another Terraform provider. Depending on the way this dependent provider initializes, you might see a
conflict arise because providers that rely on their control plane to be provisioned in another provider’s
resource can experience deadlocks in both terraform apply and terraform destroy. This
is because Terraform cannot plan resources on the control plane, which doesn’t exist yet.
What’s next? 449
Some other common scenarios that I have encountered are with the Azure Managed Grafana Service,
which provisions a hosted Grafana instance on Azure. Although this is an Azure service, it is fully
compatible with the Grafana endpoint, which means you can use the grafana provider for Terraform
to provision resources for it. This mirrors the dependency created by Azure Kubernetes Service (also
an Azure resource) and the kubernetes provider. It doesn’t matter what cloud platform you are
working with. Many cloud platforms have similar managed service offerings that are provisioned
through their corresponding provider, which produces an endpoint that can be automated by a

51906.title: masteringterraform
51906.heading: Chapter 8, where we first went through this transformation on the AWS platform. In the next section,
51906.content:
Terraform provider designed for that control plane. This is even the case with something as fun as
the minecraft provider—whether you are using EC2, Azure VMs, or GCE!
While there are two main approaches to this, both necessitate executing terraform apply multiple
times. The first approach involves provisioning each stage of our deployment independently and then
linking the upstream dependency to the downstream stage using data sources, with values provided
by input variables. This method allows different stages to be deployed relatively independently by
various teams, but it introduces additional configuration management overhead, as each downstream
dependency must explicitly reference the previously provisioned upstream stages. Consequently, this
approach results in a highly serial deployment pattern, requiring each upstream dependency to be
deployed and stabilized before progressing to the next downstream dependency:
Figure 18.6 – Current state: independent deployments with data source dependencies
An alternative approach to provisioning complex environments with Terraform diverges from independent
deployments and instead adopts a monolithic pipeline that sequentially executes terraform apply.
In this model, the dependencies are seamlessly integrated by piping the Terraform outputs from the
upstream dependency directly into the inputs of the downstream dependency. While this method
streamlines automation, it also results in a tighter coupling of the environments. Irrespective of the
approach—whether it involves independent deployments or a monolithic pipeline—there is an inherent
necessity to implement a substantial amount of glue to stitch together multiple terraform apply
steps. This entails writing Bash scripts or similar automation to act as the connective tissue, ensuring
the correct values are passed from one pipeline job to the next, thereby maintaining the integrity of
the deployment process across various stages:
Looking Ahead – Certification, Emerging Trends, and Next Steps 450
Figure 18.7 – Current state: integrated deployment with output-based dependencies
Stacks
Defined in a .tfstack file, Stacks allow you to declare one or more component blocks that
essentially define what is currently a root module. These components represent discrete and deterministic
provisioning stages within a deployment:
Figure 18.8 – Future state: Terraform Stacks
In the preceding diagram, we see three components that make up our stack:
• Network infrastructure
• Compute infrastructure
• Kubernetes deployments
This would be defined in a .tfstack file in this manner:
component "network" {
source = "./network"
What’s next? 451
inputs = {
region = var.region
}
providers = {
aws = providers.aws.this
}
}
The compute infrastructure would be defined in the same file but, this time, referencing outputs from

plan on managing complex solutions with Terraform, this is a feature to watch for in future releases!
Summary 453
Summary
In this final chapter of Mastering Terraform, we’ve explored the next steps for those of you looking to
deepen your mastery of Terraform and stay abreast of emerging trends in the community. We discussed
the importance of Terraform certification, highlighting the Associate and Professional level exams.
We also delved into Terraform Cloud, which can enhance automation and collaboration in your IaC
process, building upon the workflows and concepts we’ve covered throughout this book.
The Terraform community is vibrant and continuously evolving, with new trends and alternative
pathways emerging regularly. We explored some of the latest developments, including the Terraform
CDK, which allows you to use Terraform with familiar programming languages, and finally, we
looked at some exciting upcoming features in Terraform, such as Terraform Stacks, which promises
to revolutionize the way we manage environments through IaC by providing more flexibility and
modularity in defining and deploying sophisticated and layered cloud architectures.
Closing statement
We have traveled long, and we have traveled far. We have explored Terraform, its architecture, its
capabilities, and its form and function. Beyond just learning Terraform, to truly become masters
of Terraform, we need to ground ourselves in the architectures and work patterns expected of us as
IaC practitioners. That means we need a deep understanding of cloud architectures to effectively use
Terraform to its fullest potential. This includes the various flora and fauna we will find in the wild—
from virtual machines to containers to serverless—and all the surrounding ancillary resources that
support those architectures. Once we have this core conceptual knowledge, we’ll be able to better
navigate the multi-cloud world that we live in today and truly transcend our current cloud provider
of choice to be ready for the future—whatever may come.
Thank you for coming on this journey with me. I hope you enjoyed my very focused and practical
approach to mastering Terraform. I think the best way to learn is by doing, so I encourage you to go
to GitHub, clone any or all of the solutions described in this book, and get to work on finishing your
journey of mastering Terraform!

About the authors
Gu Huangliang is a Senior DevOps and R&D Efficiency Specialist with extensive experience
in operations and development. His work focuses on enterprise IT digital transformation and
implementation, and he is dedicated to building intelligent operations systems for businesses.
He is currently employed at a licensed financial institution.
He is included in the China Commerce Association Expert Think Tank and serves as Deputy
Director of the Think Tank Expert Committee of the National Internet Data Center Industry
Technology Innovation Strategic Alliance. He is a Candidate Expert for the Jiangsu Banking and
Insurance Industry Fintech Expert Committee, a Specially Appointed Expert for the Ministry of
Industry and Information Technology’s Enterprise Digital Transformation IOMM Committee,
a Specially Appointed Expert for the China Academy of Information and Communications
Technology’s Trusted Cloud Standard, and a Specially Appointed Expert for the China Academy
of Information and Communications Technology’s Low-Code/No-Code Promotion Center. He
is also a Tencent Cloud Most Valuable Professional (TVP) and an Alibaba Cloud Most Valuable
Professional (MVP). He is the author of the best-selling books DevOps Authoritative Guide and
Enterprise-Level DevOps Practical Cases: Continuous Delivery Edition, and a core author of the
DevOps Capability Maturity Model and Enterprise IT Operations Development White Paper. He
is a frequent speaker at technology summits.
Zheng Qingzheng is a Senior Researcher at the FinTech Research Center. He holds a Ph.D. in
Computer Science from Durham University, UK, and an M.Sc. in Computer Software Engineering
from Swansea University, UK.
He formerly served as a Technical Planning Engineer and Image Research Engineer at Huawei.
His work focuses on financial big data risk control and machine vision. He has participated in
the development of facial recognition, telecom CRM, and in-memory database systems. He has
published three papers and holds three authorized patents.
Niu Xiaoling is Chair of the DevOps Standards Working Group and Editor of DevOps
International Standards. She is a long-term researcher in DevOps, including cloud service
operations management system reviews.
She has contributed to more than 20 domestic and international standards, including the
Cloud Computing Service Agreement Reference Framework, Object Storage, Cloud Database,
DevOps Capability Maturity Model, Y.3525 Cloud Computing, Requirements for Cloud Service
Development and Operation Management, and the General Evaluation Method for Intelligent
Cloud Computing Operations. She has conducted DevOps maturity assessments for more than
50 projects and has extensive experience in standards development and evaluation testing.

and Big Data Research Institute.
They are primarily engaged in technical research and transformation consulting planning in
areas including the Enterprise Digital Transformation Maturity Model (IOMM), Trusted Digital
Services, Integrated Cloud Platforms for Digital Infrastructure, Middleware Series, Low/No-Code,
Modularization, Safe Production, and Smart Operations. Xin is responsible for developing relevant
standards, conducting evaluation and testing, and organizing technical practice exchanges.
About the reviewer
Krishna Mohan Akurathi is Director of Data Science at CVS Health. Across 16 years —
from consulting in retail, insurance, and healthcare to a decade at CVS spanning forecasting,
personalization, and customer decision science — his work has delivered $100M+ in documented
impact at $22B+ revenue scale. He has architected production ML systems (TFT, gradient boosting,
autoencoders on Azure), RAG pipelines, a Snowflake MCP server, and promo/pricing agents —
delivering self-service analytics against live warehouse data using Claude Enterprise. Krishna
holds a Master’s in Operations Research from NIT India, and serves on the HBR Advisory Council
and the AI Xecutive Council, and mentors data science and ML practitioners through Boston
University.
I would like to thank the editorial team at Packt for the opportunity to contribute to this project. The questions
this book raises — how LLMs hold up under real production conditions — are ones I encounter every day.
I hope the perspective I brought to each chapter is useful to practitioners building these systems for the first
time. I want to acknowledge my team at CVS Health — their work in production AI gave me the grounding
for this review.

Preface
Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed natural language processing and accelerated
the rise of domain-specific foundation models. Yet inside software delivery organizations, the
practical story is more complex. Many enterprises are still looking for convincing, repeatable
ways to make LLMs useful in production, not just in demonstrations or isolated experiments.
Over the last decade, software delivery itself has evolved significantly. DevOps improved build,
deployment, and collaboration practices. DevSecOps, DataOps, NoOps, MLOps, and related
practices extended this delivery ecosystem. Site Reliability Engineering renewed the focus on
reliability, stability, operational rigor, and business continuity. Platform Engineering then emerged
as a broader organizational approach, aiming to connect tools, workflows, and teams through a

51941.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51941.heading: Chapter 11: Applying LLMs in Cybersecurity 383
51941.content:
more unified, business-aware internal platform.
However, as organizations scale, the software delivery chain has also become more complex.
Delivery engineers, operations teams, testers, developers, security engineers, and project managers
are often required to work across an expanding range of tools, frameworks, processes, and
specialized workflows. This creates a growing cognitive load. The problem is no longer only a lack
of tools or features; it is the burden of learning, connecting, and operating too many fragmented
systems while still being expected to deliver reliable software and business value.
LLMs do not automatically solve this problem. Adding another chatbot or standalone model
interface will not, by itself, reduce tool sprawl or simplify delivery work. What is needed is an
integrating platform approach: one that centralizes delivery data, curates software-delivery-
specific corpora and telemetry, grounds models through retrieval and guardrails, and embeds
AI assistance into the delivery platform itself. In this view, AI support must become part of real
delivery work, including coding, testing, releasing, operating, securing, and coordinating projects,
with measurable outcomes, governance, and safe rollback.
This book is an attempt to close the gap between model capability and delivery reality. It moves
from model mechanics to enterprise readiness, and then to practical software delivery scenarios
that can be evaluated and adapted.
Preface xxiv
The goal is to help you understand not only how LLMs work, but also where they can create
measurable value inside software delivery organizations, and how they can be introduced without
increasing complexity or risk.
Who this book is for
This book is for engineers, technical leads, and practitioners working in or around DevOps, SRE,
and Platform Engineering who want to understand where LLMs fit in modern software delivery
without making existing workflows heavier or harder to manage.
It is also for anyone operating along the software delivery chain, including developers, testers,
security engineers, project managers, requirements and product roles, SRE and operations
engineers, and delivery coordinators. If your work involves pipelines, repositories, reviews,
incidents, tickets, requirements, releases, testing, security, or operational workflows, this book
is intended to help you separate durable LLM-enabled practices from hype.
The book is also relevant for LLM practitioners who understand models but need to make them
work within change-management, delivery, reliability, and governance constraints. It can also
support academic programs and training courses focused on AI-assisted software engineering,
AI-assisted delivery, or modern platform organizations.
What this book covers

51942.content:
Chapter 1, Understanding the Foundations of Large Language Models, traces the development of
language models from early theoretical and statistical approaches to neural sequence models
and LLMs. You will learn how N-gram models, HMMs, RNNs, LSTMs, and attention shaped the
path toward modern large language models.

51943.content:
Chapter 2, Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models, explains why the
Transformer became the foundation of modern LLMs. You will learn how embeddings, positional
encoding, self-attention, multi-head attention, feed-forward layers, residual connections, and
layer normalization work together inside the Transformer architecture.

51944.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51944.heading: Chapter 3, Tracing the Path from Bigram Models to GPT and ChatGPT, connects the Transformer
51944.content:
Chapter 3, Tracing the Path from Bigram Models to GPT and ChatGPT, connects the Transformer
architecture to GPT-style language generation. You will learn how a simple bigram model
illustrates next-token prediction, how GPT models generate text, and how training and generation
techniques can be improved.

51945.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51945.heading: Chapter 4, Applying Efficient Fine-Tuning Techniques to LLMs, introduces the main ways pre-trained
51945.content:
Chapter 4, Applying Efficient Fine-Tuning Techniques to LLMs, introduces the main ways pre-trained
LLMs can be adapted to specific tasks and domains. You will learn about full-parameter fine-
tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, PEFT, LoRA, QLoRA, and practical fine-tuning workflows.

51949.heading: Chapter 8, Applying LLMs in Software Testing, examines the role of LLMs in dynamic and static

Chapter 8, Applying LLMs in Software Testing, examines the role of LLMs in dynamic and static

51950.heading: Chapter 9, Applying Code LLMs in Software Development, focuses on code-focused LLMs and their
51950.content:
Chapter 9, Applying Code LLMs in Software Development, focuses on code-focused LLMs and their
use in development workflows. You will learn about large code models, representative code LLMs,
downstream coding tasks, code generation and completion, and agent-based approaches to
project-level code generation.

51951.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51951.heading: Chapter 10, Applying LLMs in Project Management, shows how LLMs can support project delivery
51951.content:
Chapter 10, Applying LLMs in Project Management, shows how LLMs can support project delivery
and coordination. You will learn how LLMs can assist with requirements analysis, task planning,
communication, collaboration, risk management, decision support, intelligent workflows, and
project management case studies.

51952.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51952.heading: Chapter 11, Applying LLMs in Cybersecurity, explores how LLMs can be applied to security workflows
51952.content:
Chapter 11, Applying LLMs in Cybersecurity, explores how LLMs can be applied to security workflows
while also introducing new risks. You will learn how LLMs can support threat detection, security
operations, alert triage, vulnerability repair, and the management of security risks introduced
by LLM adoption.
To get the most out of this book
You do not need a research lab to use this book. You should, however, have a working intuition
for how software delivery teams operate. Familiarity with delivery pipelines, code repositories,
code reviews, incidents, tickets, testing workflows, operations, and security practices will help
you connect the book’s concepts to real organizational settings.
Preface xxvi
The book was originally developed from Chinese-language material and has been translated and
adapted for a global audience, with examples and explanations adjusted where needed to make
the concepts more accessible across different software delivery contexts.
The book assumes that you want to understand both the model side and the delivery side of LLM
adoption. You will benefit from a basic awareness of LLM concepts such as Transformers, token
budgets, fine-tuning, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation, but the early chapters introduce
the necessary foundation before moving into applied delivery scenarios. If these concepts are
already familiar, you may move more quickly through the foundation chapters and focus on the
practice chapters.
Code examples and implementation patterns are presented so they can be adapted to mainstream
software delivery stacks. When a concept depends on an infrastructure assumption, that
assumption is called out. The emphasis is not on one fixed toolchain, but on helping you
understand the principles, constraints, workflows, and evaluation points needed to apply LLMs
responsibly in software delivery contexts.

In this first part, you will build the technical foundation needed to understand how large language

This foundation also includes fine-tuning, because understanding LLMs is not complete without

Understanding the Foundations
of Large Language Models
Large language models (LLMs) did not appear suddenly. They are the result of decades of progress
in natural language processing, from early theoretical models of information and probability to
statistical language models, neural networks, and large-scale pre-trained systems such as BERT
and GPT. Understanding this development path is important because it shows what problems
earlier models tried to solve, where they were limited, and why modern LLMs represent such a
major shift in how machines process language.
This chapter introduces the foundations of LLMs by tracing the evolution of language modeling
techniques. You will first examine the major stages in the development of natural language
processing, then explore important pre-LLM models such as N-gram models, Hidden Markov
Models, RNNs, and LSTMs. Finally, you will compare HMMs and N-gram models to understand
how different modeling assumptions shape the way language systems process sequences.
In this chapter, we will be covering the following main topics:
• Tracing the development of LLMs
• Exploring foundational NLP models before LLMs
• Introducing neural networks for sequence modeling
• Addressing long-sequence challenges with LSTMs

Tracing the development of LLMs

After entering the 21st century, Apple released the first iPhone in 2007, swiftly heralding the era of

they accessed information, until 2020, when OpenAI released GPT-3 — an event that marked the

The arrival of the AI era is an important turning point in the development of human society. In

gap harder to close. AI models are the core element of the new era, and technology practitioners

To understand how LLMs became possible, it is useful to look at the major stages of natural
language processing (NLP) that came before them. Each stage introduced a different way of
modeling language, moving from theoretical foundations to statistical methods, neural networks,
and finally large-scale pre-trained language models.
Mapping the evolution of NLP models
Before LLMs emerged, NLP models experienced several stages of development. The following
are some crucial stages.

51956.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51956.heading: Chapter 1 5
51956.content:
Chapter 1 5
Establishing theoretical foundations for language models
Theoretical models, represented by Shannon’s information theory, study the information
quantity and entropy of natural language. In 1948, Shannon applied Markov process models to
natural language modeling and proposed extending the concept of entropy from thermodynamics
to the field of natural language modeling.
These early theoretical ideas provided a foundation for treating language as information that
could be measured and modeled. As computing resources became available, researchers began
applying statistical methods to model word sequences and speech patterns more directly.
Applying statistical models to natural language processing
The representative models of this stage are the N-gram model and the Hidden Markov Model
(HMM). The N-gram model is a relatively simple statistical language model, which assumes that
the probability of a word occurring depends only on the previous N-1 words. It is used for text
prediction. HMM is a statistical model for handling sequential data and is suitable for tasks such
as speech recognition and machine translation.
Statistical models made language processing more practical, but they still relied heavily on fixed
assumptions and manually designed probabilities. As machine learning advanced, neural network
models offered a way to learn richer representations from data.
Introducing neural networks for sequence modeling
The representative models of this stage are the Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) and the
Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). RNNs can handle sequential data and are suitable for
tasks such as machine translation and speech recognition. CNNs can process image data and are
suitable for text classification, sentiment analysis, and other tasks.
Neural network models improved the ability to process sequences and learn patterns from
language, but larger datasets and greater computing power enabled a further shift. This led to
the development of pre-trained language models and eventually LLMs, which could learn broad
language representations from massive corpora.
Scaling toward LLMs
Representative models of this stage include BERT and GPT-3, among others. BERT is a pre-trained
language model released by Google AI in 2018, and it has attracted widespread attention due to
its outstanding language understanding capabilities. The advent of BERT marks the transition
of the natural language processing field from traditional manual feature engineering to the deep
learning era.
Understanding the Foundations of Large Language Models 6
According to the implementation sequence of key algorithmic models, the development trajectory
of natural language models is shown in Figure 1.1. The graph shows the history of NLP models
and the required computing power from 1950 to 2020. The computational power data in Figure

As explained above, NLP is founded on theory. With limited computing power, statistical methods
were employed to model natural language. As computing power increased, neural network models
were gradually applied to the field of natural language processing. With the realization of even
greater computational power, LLMs emerged, marking the entrance of natural language processing
into the AI era.
Although we have entered the era of LLMs, traditional natural language processing models still
possess unique advantages, such as low computational resource consumption and fast response
speed. In practical applications, the appropriate model should be selected based on the specific
task requirements.

51958.heading: Chapter 1 7
51958.content:
Chapter 1 7
With this historical progression in mind, the next section looks more closely at the foundational
models that shaped NLP before the rise of modern LLMs. Understanding models such as N-grams,
HMMs, RNNs, and LSTMs will make it easier to see what problems LLMs were designed to
overcome and why earlier approaches still matter in some practical scenarios.
Exploring foundational NLP models before LLMs
Before modern LLMs, NLP relied on simpler statistical and sequence-based models to represent
language, predict words, and infer hidden patterns from observed data. This section introduces
two important foundational approaches: N-gram models, which predict language based on
observed word frequencies, and Hidden Markov Models (HMM), which use hidden states and
transition probabilities to model sequences. Understanding these models helps clarify what
earlier NLP systems could do well, where they were limited, and why later neural models became
necessary.
Understanding N-gram models
In the field of natural language processing, the N-gram model is a relatively simple statistical
language model. It is based on the Markov assumption, which means the probability of a word
appearing depends only on the previous N-1 words. The formula for the N-gram model is as follows:
𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃 𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃 𝑃 𝑃 𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃 𝑃 𝑃 𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃 𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃 𝑃 𝑃 𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃 𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃 𝑃 𝑃 𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃
In this equation, w 1, w 2, …, w n is a word sequence of length n, C (w 1, w 2, …, w n) is the number of
occurrences of this sequence in the corpus, and C (w 1, w 2, …, w n-1) is the number of occurrences of
the previous n-1 words of this sequence in the corpus. The number of parameters in the N-gram
model increases exponentially with N, so in practice, 2-gram or 3-gram models are usually used.
From the perspective of understanding the basic concepts, we can temporarily ignore the complex
principles behind the formula and directly discuss how the N-gram model is used in practice.
Suppose there is a chain composed of multiple words; the N-gram algorithm observes units
made up of every N consecutive words in that chain to predict which word may appear in the next
group of words. This is where the name “N-gram” comes from, with “gram” referring to a word.
For example, when you say the phrase “I like to eat,” and there is previously a phrase like “I like to
eat apples,” the N-gram model may predict the next word to be “apples” because in previous data,
“apples” often appears after “I like to eat.” This is why the N-gram model is used for text prediction.
Understanding the Foundations of Large Language Models 8
The design of the N-gram model is quite straightforward: it is similar to a large table that records
the frequency of different word combinations. For a 2-gram (i.e., Bigram), the table records the

51959.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51959.heading: Chapter 1 7
51959.content:
probability of every pair of words; for a 3-gram (i.e., Trigram), it records the probability for every
three-word combination, and so on. When designing this model, you only need to determine the
value of N, that is, how many words to consider as a group to predict the next word, then collect
data and fill in the probability table.
Although the N-gram model is somewhat outdated, it still performs well in certain specific
scenarios. For example, in some vertical domains, the N-gram model can achieve good results
through training on large amounts of data. In resource-limited situations, the N-gram model can
achieve satisfactory results with less training data. In scenarios that require a fast response time,
the N-gram model can deliver good results with relatively little computation.
Applying N-gram models in practical scenarios
Because N-gram models are simple, fast, and based on frequency statistics, they remain useful in
tasks where lightweight prediction is more important than deep contextual understanding. The
following examples show where this type of model can still be applied effectively.
Spelling check and error correction
The N-gram model can be used to predict the probability of word sequences, thereby supporting
tasks such as speech recognition and machine translation. By comparing the probabilities of
different word sequences, it is possible to infer which sequence is more likely to be the user’s
intended input. For example, if a user types “spel checker”, the N-gram model can determine
that the sequence “spell checker” is more common than “spel checker”, thus suggesting the
correct spelling.
So, in spelling correction, the model compares the likelihood of different word sequences and
selects the one that appears more probable based on previous data. A similar principle can also be
applied to simple text generation, where the model predicts likely next words from recent input.
Text generation
Although deep learning models have made significant progress in text generation, the N-gram
model still has practical applications in certain simple scenarios or resource-constrained
situations. For instance, in predictive text functions for keyboard applications or auto-reply for
simple chatbots, the N-gram model can quickly generate text suggestions based on previous inputs.
Beyond these examples, the main strengths and limitations of N-gram models can be summarized
through their key characteristics.

51960.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51960.heading: Chapter 1 9
51960.content:
Chapter 1 9
Characteristics of N-gram models
The above examples show how N-gram models use frequency patterns for lightweight prediction.
Their main strengths and limitations can be summarized through the following characteristics:
• Prediction based on frequency statistics: The N-gram model predicts the next word
according to the occurrence probability of lexical sequences. The model assumes that the
appearance of the current word depends only on the previous N-1 words.
• The N-gram model is stateless: In the N-gram model, there is no explicit definition of
“state”; the model directly operates on the observed sequences (such as words in text).
Each part of the sequence is considered independently.
• Simplicity and computational efficiency: The design and implementation of the N-gram
model are relatively simple, and computational efficiency is high, but as N increases, the
model’s size and complexity grow dramatically.
N-gram models work directly with observed word sequences and use frequency statistics to
predict what may come next. Hidden Markov Models take a different approach: they assume
that an observed sequence is generated by an underlying sequence of hidden states. This makes
HMMs useful for tasks where the system must infer something not directly visible from the data
that can be observed.
Understanding Hidden Markov Models
Apart from the N-gram model based on statistical thinking, the Hidden Markov Model (HMM)
is also an important model in natural language processing. The basic idea of HMM is to assume
that the observed sequence is generated by an unobservable state sequence, and the transitions
of the state sequence follow a Markov chain. The formula of HMM is as follows:
𝑃𝑃(𝑂𝑂 𝑂 𝑂𝑂) = ∑
𝑄𝑄
𝑃𝑃(𝑂𝑂|𝑄𝑄)𝑃𝑃 (𝑄𝑄|𝑂𝑂) 
In this equation, P(Q|I) is the probability of the state sequence Q under condition I, and P(O|Q)
is the probability of the observed sequence O given the state sequence Q. The purpose of the
summation is to compute the probability of the observed sequence O under all possible state
sequences Q. The parameters of HMM include the state transition probability matrix, observation
probability matrix, and initial state probability vector. The training process of HMM usually uses
the Baum-Welch algorithm, and the decoding process generally uses the Viterbi algorithm.
Understanding the Foundations of Large Language Models 10
The above formulas and algorithms may seem rather abstract, but you can better understand the
usage of HMM from practical application perspectives.
Applying HMMs in practical scenarios
The idea of hidden states becomes easier to understand through practical examples. In each case,
the model observes available evidence and uses it to infer an underlying condition or intention
that cannot be seen directly.

51961.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51961.heading: Chapter 1 9
51961.content:
Weather forecasting
Imagine you are an ancient meteorologist who cannot directly know whether tomorrow’s weather
will be sunny, cloudy, or rainy. However, you can infer tomorrow’s weather by observing natural
phenomena, such as bird behavior, wind direction, and the shape of clouds. In this scenario,
tomorrow’s weather (sunny, cloudy, rainy) belongs to the hidden states, as you cannot directly
access it; whereas the behaviors of birds, wind direction, and cloud formations are observable
states, as these can be directly observed. HMM can help you predict tomorrow’s weather (hidden
state) based on the observed natural phenomena (observable states). By learning from historical
data, HMM understands the transition probabilities between different weather states (for example,
the probability that a sunny day turns into a cloudy day) as well as the probability of observing
certain natural phenomena under specific weather conditions (such as the probability of seeing
specific bird behaviors on a Sunny day). Therefore, even if you cannot directly observe tomorrow’s
weather, you can still make the most likely prediction based on today’s observations.
Weather forecasting illustrates the general idea of hidden-state inference: the model uses visible
clues to estimate an unseen condition. A similar idea can be applied to text input, where the system
observes what the user has typed and infers the most likely intended continuation.
Intelligent recommendations
When using the keyboard app on a smartphone and you start typing “I want to eat,” the keyboard
automatically suggests possible words for you, such as “apple,” “pizza,” or “ice cream.” In this
context, the keyboard app uses HMM to predict which word you are most likely to type next. In this
example, the sequence of words you actually intend to enter (like “I want to eat pizza”) belongs
to the hidden states, because the keyboard app cannot directly access your thoughts, while the
words you have actually typed (“I want to eat”) are the observable states, which the app can
directly obtain. By analyzing large amounts of text data, HMM learns the transition probabilities
between words (for example, the probability that “I want to eat” is followed by “pizza”) as well
as the probability that the next word appears given a sequence. Therefore, even though the app
does not know your exact intention, it can use your input and the learned language model to
recommend the most suitable word for you.

51962.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51962.heading: Chapter 1 11
51962.content:
Chapter 1 11
N-gram models and HMMs are both effective tools for processing sequence data, widely used in
NLP and other fields. Although there are certain similarities between them, they have significant
differences in theoretical foundations and applications. HMMs focus on state transition
probabilities and the probability of observations given a state. By analyzing observed data, HMMs
infer the sequence of hidden states that cannot be directly observed and are commonly used in
application scenarios such as weather prediction and text input.
Characteristics of HMMs
From these examples, we can identify the features that distinguish HMMs from simpler sequence
models:
• State-based and transitions: HMM is a state-based probabilistic model, where the
sequence of states is hidden and cannot be directly observed. The model infers these
hidden states from the observed sequence (such as words or phonemes).
• HMMs have states: HMMs define hidden states and the transition probabilities between
these states. Each state is associated with a set of possible observations, which are defined
by an observation probability distribution.
• Complexity and powerful modeling capability: HMMs can model the complex processes
underlying observed sequences. Although their training and inference are more complex
than N-gram models, they are able to capture deeper sequential dependencies.
N-gram models and HMMs both process sequential data, but they differ in how they represent
that data. N-gram models work directly with observed word sequences, while HMMs separate
observed signals from hidden states. The next section compares these two approaches in terms
of observations, states, dependencies, and typical application areas.
Comparing HMMs and N-gram models
The main theoretical differences between HMM and N-gram models are as follows:
• Observations and states: N-gram models act directly on the observed sequence, whereas
HMMs distinguish between the observed sequence and the hidden state sequence.
• Dependencies: The dependencies in N-gram models are relatively simple and limited
to a fixed length (N-1), while the state transitions in HMMs can capture longer-term
dependencies, and the model structure allows for more flexible sequential dependency
modeling.
Understanding the Foundations of Large Language Models 12
• Range of application: Due to these differences, HMMs are generally used for more complex
tasks, such as speech recognition or sequence alignment in bioinformatics, where the
model needs to infer underlying structures behind observed data. N-gram models, on
the other hand, are more suitable for tasks that directly predict based on sequential data,
such as text generation or simpler language models.
N-gram models and HMMs show how earlier NLP systems handled sequences through frequency

51963.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51963.heading: Chapter 1 11
51963.content:
statistics, hidden states, and transition probabilities. However, these approaches relied on fixed
assumptions and could not learn flexible contextual representations directly from large amounts
of data. Neural network models introduced a new direction by learning sequence patterns from
data, which is the focus of the next section.
Introducing neural networks for sequence modeling
Early developments of statistical models only considered frequency statistics and did not fully
take into account the temporal relationships in sequence data. HMMs introduced the concept
of state transition probabilities, thereby gaining a preliminary ability to predict based on state
changes. However, the state transition probabilities in HMMs are fixed and cannot be dynamically
adjusted based on the temporal dependencies in sequence data. For time series processing tasks,
such as language modeling, speech recognition, or any form of time series analysis, the stateless
nature of HMMs limits their effectiveness, as processing sequence data often relies on contextual
information. The design inspiration for Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) comes from the way
the human brain processes sequential information, especially its ability to maintain information
states through time. By introducing recurrence, RNNs are able to retain information in their
internal states, enabling them to dynamically process varying sequence lengths and capture
temporal dependencies in time series data. This structure allows RNNs to pass information from
the past to the current task, resulting in more effective learning and prediction. The basic structure
of an RNN is shown in Figure 1.2.
Figure 1.2: Basic structure of an RNN

51964.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51964.heading: Chapter 1 13
51964.content:
Chapter 1 13
Figure 1.2 shows a simple RNN structure, illustrating three consecutive time steps as an RNN
processes sequence data.
• x t denotes the input at time step t. This is the current element of the sequence received
by the network.
• h represents the hidden layer of the network, which is the core of the RNN. The hidden
layer can transmit information between different time steps, thereby retaining information
from previous inputs.
• h t-1, h t, h t+1 respectively represent the hidden states at time steps t-1, t, and t+1. Each hidden
state h t is calculated based on the previous step’s hidden state h t-1 and the current input x t.
• o denotes the output layer, which generates output at each time step.
• o t-1, o t, o t+1 denote the outputs at time steps t-1, t, and t+1, respectively. The output is usually
computed based on the current time step’s hidden state h t.
The function of an RNN is to process sequence data, making it particularly suitable for tasks such
as time series analysis, speech recognition, and language modeling. By maintaining hidden states,
RNNs can capture the temporal dependencies in sequences, thereby generating or predicting the
next element in the sequence. This structure enables RNNs to take previous contextual information
into account for more accurate predictions in sequential tasks.
Although RNNs improved on earlier statistical models by maintaining information across time
steps, their recurrent structure also introduced training difficulties. These limitations become
especially clear when RNNs process long sequences, where gradients must pass through many
repeated time steps during training.
Identifying the limitations of RNNs
RNNs have two major architectural limitations:
• Vanishing gradient: RNNs are prone to the vanishing gradient problem during training.
This occurs because the gradients of RNNs are computed through BackPropagation
Through Time (BPTT), and during backpropagation, the gradient is repeatedly multiplied
by a value less than 1, causing the gradient to gradually disappear.
• Exploding Gradient: RNNs are also susceptible to the exploding gradient problem during
training. This happens because the gradients are calculated through backpropagation
through time, and in this process, the gradients are continually multiplied by a value
greater than 1, causing the gradients to rapidly explode.
Understanding the Foundations of Large Language Models 14
These problems are mainly caused by the recurrent connections in the RNN structure and the
use of saturated activation functions such as tanh or sigmoid. In long sequences, as gradients are
backpropagated to earlier layers, the chain rule is applied multiple times, causing the gradients
to be multiplied by a series of weight matrices and accumulated over multiple time steps. If the

51965.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51965.heading: Chapter 1 13
51965.content:
values in these weight matrices are less than 1, the gradients will gradually decay, leading to
vanishing gradients; if the values are greater than 1, the gradients will grow rapidly, resulting in
exploding gradients.
These training challenges made it difficult for standard RNNs to retain useful information over long
sequences. LSTMs were introduced to address this problem by adding a memory cell and gating
mechanisms that control how information is stored, updated, and passed forward through time.
Addressing long-sequence challenges with LSTMs
LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) networks are a special type of RNN, specifically designed to
solve the problems of gradient vanishing and gradient explosion that occur when RNNs process
long sequence data. LSTM addresses these issues by introducing key structures. Figure 1.3 shows
a simple internal structure of an LSTM.
Figure 1.3: Internal structure of LSTM
To understand how LSTMs address the limitations of standard RNNs, it is useful to examine the
internal components that control memory over time. The memory cell and its gates determine
what information is retained, updated, forgotten, and passed forward through the sequence.

51966.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51966.heading: Chapter 1 15
51966.content:
Chapter 1 15
Explaining the LSTM memory cell and gates
The core of LSTM is a structure called the memory cell, which can retain information over long
sequence data. The memory cell consists of an internal state called the cell state and an external
state called the hidden state. The cell state can transmit information between time steps, thus
maintaining memory of previous inputs. The hidden state is calculated based on the current input
and the hidden state from the previous time step. The memory cell of the LSTM also includes
three gates: forget gate, input gate, and output gate. These gates control the updating of the
cell state and the output of the hidden state, allowing LSTMs to capture temporal dependencies
in long sequence data:
• Forget gate: Applies a sigmoid function to a linear transformation of the cell state from the
previous time step and the current time step’s input to compute the forget probability. This
is then multiplied element-wise to decide which information to forget from the cell state.
• Input gate: Uses sigmoid and tanh functions to control which information to update and
how to update it, combining the previous time step’s cell state and the current time step’s
input to form a new cell state.
• Output gate: Uses a sigmoid function to perform a linear transformation of the current
time step’s cell state to determine the output probability, which is then multiplied element-
wise to decide which information to output.
The roles of the forget gate, input gate, and output gate are not just to “decide” what operations to
perform on certain information, but rather to control the flow of information via learned weights.
In addition to introducing the gating mechanism, LSTM also implements other improvements
such as peephole connections and coupled forget gates:
• Peephole connections: Through peephole connections, the forget gate can directly access
the memory cell state C t at the current time step to decide how much information to forget,
thereby controlling the information flow more precisely.
• Coupled forget gates allow for more effective handling of noise in the input sequence. A
typical application scenario is the “machine translation task.” LSTM can remember the
semantics and structure of sentences in the source language and retain this information
during translation, thus generating more accurate translation results.
These mechanisms improved the ability of recurrent models to preserve information over longer
sequences, but they did not remove all practical limitations. Researchers therefore proposed
related architectures and extensions that made recurrent sequence models more efficient, more
context-aware, and better suited to complex language tasks.
Understanding the Foundations of Large Language Models 16
Connecting LSTM variants to attention

51967.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51967.heading: Chapter 1 15
51967.content:
LSTM also has some issues in practical applications, for which researchers have proposed several
improved models. Figure 1.4 shows three branch models of LSTM:
Figure 1.4: Three branch models of LSTM
The three important branches of LSTM are described as follows:
• Gated Recurrent Unit: A simplified version of LSTM with fewer parameters and faster
training speed, suitable for scenarios that require higher speed and efficiency, such as
speech recognition.
• Attention Mechanism: Enables the model to focus on the parts of the input sequence most
relevant to the current output, suitable for tasks like text summarization and machine
translation.
• Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory Network: Able to process sequence data by
simultaneously utilizing both past and future information, suitable for scenarios that
require modeling global dependencies in the input sequence, such as sentiment analysis
and text classification.
Among these branches, the attention mechanism became especially important. It allowed
sequence models to focus on the parts of the input that were most relevant to the current output,
improving performance on tasks such as summarization and machine translation. This idea was
later developed further in the Transformer architecture, where attention became the central
mechanism for processing language.

51968.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51968.heading: Chapter 1 17
51968.content:

Understanding the Transformer
Architecture Behind Large
Language Models
In the field of modern natural language processing, with the rapid development of deep learning
technology, traditional sequence models such as RNN and LSTM have gradually exposed efficiency
and performance bottlenecks, especially when dealing with long-distance dependencies. The serial
computation characteristic of these models leads to inefficiency in both training and inference
processes. To address this issue, the Google AI team proposed the Transformer model in 2017.
This groundbreaking innovation has completely changed the way sequential data is processed.
By introducing the self-attention mechanism, the Transformer model not only overcomes the
limitations of traditional models but also lays the foundation for the future of natural language
processing. Today, the latest large language models are all built on this architecture. An in-depth
study of the principles and applications of the Transformer model is not only key to understanding
contemporary natural language processing technology but also an important step for the future
development of artificial intelligence.
